description: Dedicated to make space exploration intuitive. We bridge the gap between open NASA data and interactive , userfriendly tools.
summary:
TERRASCOPE is an interactive global decision-support web application and satellite mapping engine that identifies and characterizes overlooked terrestrial analog sites for future Moon and Mars landing sites and permanent bases.

While classic testbeds like the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Death Valley are already well-studied, our tool spotlights new, under-characterized environments across deserts, polar regions, volcanic terrains, and subsurface caves. Users input custom mission requirements—or click any coordinate on Earth—to sample live NASA POWER satellite climatology and 90-meter digital elevation data alongside multi-agency planetary datasets (NASA, ISRO, ESA, and JAXA). The engine ranks optimal Earth matches across four core pillars: topography, geology, environment, and available ISRU resources.

Validating rovers, drills, and habitats in accurate terrestrial analogs drastically reduces mission risk and cost before launch. By pairing ranked site recommendations with actionable field-testing protocols and transparently quantifying Earth's simulation gaps (such as gravity, vacuum, and radiation limits), TERRASCOPE helps mission planners rigorously test hardware for safe, sustainable lunar and Martian exploration.
details:
What TERRASCOPE Does & How It Works

TERRASCOPE is an interactive global planetary analog search engine and decision-support web application designed to identify, evaluate, and characterize Earth locations that simulate conditions on the Moon and Mars.

Instead of presenting a static catalog, TERRASCOPE operates through a dual-mode analytical workflow:

  1. Multi-Criteria Global Trade-Study Search: Mission planners configure their target destination (Moon or Mars), site architecture (Landing Site or Permanent Base), terrain environment (preset categories or custom user-defined text), ISRU resource priority, and environmental thresholds (mean surface temperature, precipitation/aridity, and minimum elevation). A weighted scoring engine evaluates global candidate sites across four core pillars—Topography, Geology, Environment, and Available Resources (ISRU)—and ranks the optimal terrestrial matches.
  2. "Click-Anywhere-on-Earth" Live Satellite Sampler: Users can click any coordinate on the interactive satellite world map to trigger real-time API queries to the NASA POWER Satellite Climatology API and Copernicus 90-meter Digital Elevation Model (DEM), computing live surface temperature, solar irradiance, precipitation, elevation, and local slope angles on the fly.

For every matched location, TERRASCOPE pairs the Earth site with its lunar or Martian twin, generates a mission-specific engineering test protocol, provides direct links to NASA Moon/Mars Trek and 3D Google Earth, and explicitly documents Characterization Gaps—detailing physical factors Earth cannot replicate (such as 1/6g or 3/8g gravity, ultra-high vacuum, and cosmic radiation) alongside engineering mitigations.

Benefits of TERRASCOPE

  • De-Risks Hardware Prior to Launch: Helps engineering teams validate percussive rock drills, rover wheel traction, LiDAR/SLAM cave-mapping drones, dust seals, and ISRU extraction systems in geophysically matched field sites before spaceflight.
  • Uncovers Overlooked Global Testbeds: Includes a "New Analogs Only" filter that excludes heavily studied benchmarks (the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Death Valley) by default, spotlighting under-characterized sites across all seven continents such as Puga Valley (Ladakh), Lonar Impact Crater, Undara Lava Tubes, Lanzarote, and the Qaidam Basin.
  • Transparent Scientific Honesty: Prevents false confidence by breaking down similarity scores pillar-by-pillar and highlighting simulation limits so engineers know when to pair field tests with vacuum chambers or gravity-offloading rigs.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Runs directly in any web browser with live satellite telemetry, requiring no specialized GIS software installation.

Intended Impact

TERRASCOPE is built to support aerospace mission planners, planetary scientists, university rover teams, and space agencies preparing for Artemis lunar surface operations and future Mars exploration. By standardizing how terrestrial analog sites are scored, compared, and documented—and by expanding analog discovery to diverse, under-studied regions worldwide—TERRASCOPE lowers the barrier to rigorous pre-flight field testing and fosters broader global participation in planetary exploration.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Mapping & Geospatial Visualization: Leaflet.js (interactive map engine and coordinate sampling) and Esri World Imagery satellite tiles.
  • Live Data APIs & Interactive Portals: NASA POWER Project Climatology REST API, Open-Meteo Elevation API (serving ESA Copernicus 90m DEM data), OpenStreetMap Nominatim (reverse geocoding), NASA Solar System Treks (Moon Trek & Mars Trek), and Google Earth Web.
  • Planetary Reference Datasets: NASA Planetary Data System (LRO LOLA/Diviner, MRO CRISM/HiRISE, Mars Odyssey GRS, ICESat-2), ISRO Chandrayaan-1 M3& Chandrayaan-2 IIRS, ESA Mars Express, and JAXA Kaguya (SELENE).
  • Software & Hosting: Plain-text code editor, web browser developer tools, and Netlify (cloud web hosting and deployment).
  • Hardware: Standard consumer laptops used for software development, live API verification, and demo recording.

How TERRASCOPE Is Creative

  • Hybrid Live-Satellite + Planetary-Twin Engine: Rather than functioning as a static atlas or simple quiz, TERRASCOPE pairs curated multi-agency planetary science with live real-time satellite telemetry, enabling users to sample any point on Earth instantaneously.
  • Architecture-Aware Dynamic Weighting: Switching between Landing Site and Permanent Base automatically shifts the mathematical weights of the scoring algorithm—prioritizing flat touchdown slopes (<10°) and plume-impingement stability for landers, versus natural radiation shielding and extractable ISRU resources for permanent bases.
  • Custom User-Defined Criteria Parser: Allows users to type free-form terrain descriptions or hardware goals (such as "3D-printed sintered bricks" or "subsurface lava tubes") instead of restricting searches to fixed dropdown options.
  • First-Class "Simulation Gap" Analysis: Integrates Earth's physical limitations directly into every result card as an actionable engineering checklist.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • The Four Core Analog Pillars: Topography (elevation, slope gradient, surface roughness), Geology (host lithology, impact breccia, tholeiitic basalt, evaporites, lava tubes), Environment (mean surface temperature, precipitation/aridity, solar flux, UV exposure), and Available Resources / ISRU (water-ice deposits, ilmenite for oxygen extraction, natural cavern shielding, biosignature-bearing salts).
  • Over-Characterization Bias: Separating classic analog benchmarks (Atacama, Haughton Crater, Death Valley) from lesser-known terrestrial sites to directly fulfill the challenge's goal of identifying new analogs.
  • Earth-to-Space Scaling Physics: Accounting for gravitational differences (9.81 m/s² Earth vs. 1.62m/s² Moon and 3.72 m/s² Mars), atmospheric pressure regimes (101.3 kPa vs. lunar vacuum and 0.6 kPa CO2, and terrestrial weathering vs. unweathered extraterrestrial regolith.
